absent: Numeric values of clock identifiers, device states, broadcast modes, error codes and tick constants beyond the names shown.
Internal behavior of alarm firing, RTC interface setup, suspend and resume handlers, and the underlying alarm sleep wait.
Locking and ordering for timerqueue manipulation and concurrent alarm base access outside initialization and resume.
Full tick device setup, replacement scoring, broadcast mask maintenance and clock notification effects.
High-resolution activation criteria and next-event selection and reprogramming policy.
Time-namespace conversion, leap-second scheduling and jiffies sequence update discipline.

findings.text: Legacy user time output adapts to the build time model. In 64-bit compatibility mode the kernel 64-bit value is transferred unchanged to user memory, otherwise seconds and nanoseconds are narrowed into the legacy pair before transfer. User copy failure is signaled as a fault and success as zero.

Narrowing from kernel to legacy representation preserves the seconds and nanoseconds magnitudes carried in the source, with no renormalization shown. The only failure mode in the fragments is inability to write the destination.

Alarm sleep requires RTC backing, flags limited to the absolute marker, and wake-alarm privilege. Relative requests resolve against the selected base current time with saturating addition, while absolute requests undergo time-namespace conversion. Interruptible relative waits preserve type and deadline for restart; absolute waits do not produce remaining time.
Restart of an interrupted alarm sleep reconstitutes a temporary stack alarm of the saved type with the standard wake handler and reissues the underlying wait for the saved absolute deadline.
Alarm clock descriptor exposes resolution query plus current-time access in numeric and broken-down forms, binding the alarm family to the generic clock query path.
Alarm clock descriptor covers timer object lifecycle and status through creation, update, removal and query operations shared with common timer helpers where applicable.
Alarm clock descriptor covers arming control through arm, rearm, forward, remaining, cancel-attempt and quiesce operations plus a dedicated sleep entry, delegating queueing to alarm-specific helpers.
Alarm timer platform integration uses a power-management table binding suspend and resume handlers and a platform driver named for the alarm timer linked to that table.
Boot-time broken-down read combines the boot clock read with a time-namespace adjustment for the caller.

Initialization establishes real-time and boot-time bases with matching clock identities and accessors, prepares per-base timer queues and spin locks, then brings up the RTC interface before registering the platform driver, unwinding the interface if registration fails.

Stack-based initialization for alarms and high-resolution timers binds the embedded timer in absolute mode using the clock selected by the alarm type and associates the requested callback. Debug preparation precedes core timer setup.
Debug preparation for stack timers is configuration dependent: one variant registers the object with the debug facility and emits a setup trace, the other performs no observable action.
Minimum delta limit equals the number of nanoseconds in one second divided by the kernel tick frequency.

Tick-to-nanosecond conversion scales the latch by shift then divides by multiplier, clamping on shift overflow and flooring tiny results at one microsecond. A missing multiplier is treated as unity with a warning. Rounding-up applies for minimum calculations and conditionally for maximum calculations on slower devices, and is skipped when it would overflow.
Public delta conversion exposes the internal converter in minimum mode, inheriting its scaling, clamping and flooring contract.
Unbind helper record pairs a clock-event device reference with an integer outcome code.
A global clock-events mutex serializes device list circulation including the released-list drain that returns devices to the main list for reevaluation.

Alarm bases each carry a spin lock initialized at startup. Broadcast publication, mode changes and periodic restart are serialized by a raw broadcast lock held with interrupts saved, while module reference release for a replaced device occurs after that lock is dropped.

High-resolution base offset refresh requires the per-CPU base lock held, with interrupt state already disabled on resume. Timekeeper reads use sequence protection with retry, gated by a clock-was-set sequence, and tick period reads use the jiffies sequence.

Clock-event devices move among detached, shutdown, periodic and oneshot conditions: released devices become detached, newcomers are shut down on admission, and tick setup selects periodic only when periodic-capable and broadcast oneshot is inactive, otherwise oneshot. Shutdown also parks the next deadline at its maximum and clears the forced flag.

Broadcast scope toggles between periodic and oneshot modes with explicit switch handling and per-mode resume restart. One-shot broadcast resume and one-shot setup each have a configuration variant that is a no-op or a trap respectively.
System resume coverage for time includes both broadcast and local tick domains. Configurations without broadcast support provide empty placeholders for broadcast, local-oneshot and top-level resume.

Broadcast resume reawakens the broadcast device when present and, only when the broadcast mask is non-empty, restarts periodic operation or reasserts oneshot operation according to the current broadcast mode.

Local resume reawakens the per-CPU event device, then when the CPU is not covered by broadcast it reestablishes periodic timing or reprograms oneshot to current time. Broadcast membership depends on mode and mask, with a non-broadcast configuration reporting no membership.

Periodic setup assigns the appropriate periodic handler, ignores dummy devices, and either enters periodic mode or emulates periodicity by repeatedly programming oneshot deadlines advanced by one tick until accepted, using a sequence-protected read of the next period.

Handler assignment distinguishes broadcast from local delivery, with a simplified variant always selecting local handling. Device usability excludes dummy capability. Broadcast oneshot activity reflects the broadcast mode, with a non-broadcast configuration reporting inactive.

High-resolution resume refreshes clock offsets and then either forces reprogramming when high-resolution operation is active or refreshes the next-event cache otherwise, all while holding the base lock.
Base refresh propagates real-time, boot-time and adjusted-time offsets obtained from the timekeeper into both hard and soft expiry domains and returns the current monotonic reading.

Monotonic-plus-offset read samples the timekeeper under sequence protection, refreshes cached offsets only when the set-sequence changed, and applies a one-second leap correction to the real offset when at or beyond the leap instant.

New device evaluation prefers per-CPU replacement when the replacement test succeeds, handling module acquisition and prior-device handoff plus oneshot notification, and otherwise falls back to considering the device for broadcast use.

Device exchange detaches and queues any outgoing device for deferred handling while requiring an incoming device to start detached before it is shut down. The outgoing module reference is released as part of the handoff.

Broadcast admission first offers the device as a wakeup source, then applies feature and rating gates, publishes the winner with a neutral handler assigned to its predecessor, restarts periodic output when interested CPUs exist, and follows oneshot-specific activation or global notification as appropriate.

Broadcast candidacy rejects dummy, per-CPU and deep-idle-limited devices, requires oneshot capability once broadcast is in oneshot mode, and otherwise prefers a strictly higher rating over the incumbent.

Per-CPU wakeup candidacy requires per-CPU oneshot capability without dummy or deep-idle limitations, an exact CPU mask match and a superior rating, with the winner receiving the wakeup handler. One configuration never selects a wakeup device and always reports none.

User copies can fault, stack alarms must not outlive their frame, module acquisition can refuse a device, oneshot programming may need deadline advancement, resume assumes interrupts disabled, delta math must survive overflow and tiny values, and one oneshot-setup variant traps rather than operating.
